metadata.title: The secret behind Singapore’s success: identifying the top predictors of student reading achievement using machine learning
metadata.venue: Journal for the Study of Education and Development: Infancia y Aprendizaje

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 microdata for Singapore, with students nested in schools (166 schools; 6,676 students). The authors describe using PISA’s complex survey design guidance for descriptive statistics and correlations, employing R packages intsvy, survey, and svyPVpack to follow the PISA manual’s plausible-value aggregation procedure. However, for the primary machine-learning model (Random Forest regression), the manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights, and it explicitly uses only the first plausible value rather than aggregating across all 10 PVs. Therefore, the ML stage appears to be an unweighted, flat modeling approach on the selected PV, which may under-correct for the nested sampling structure compared with fully weight-aware PV-based estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the publicly available PISA 2018 dataset for Singapore. The analytic sample consists of 15-year-old students (Singapore participants) nested in 166 schools. The outcome is PISA 2018 reading literacy, and the study focuses on questionnaire-derived predictor variables mapped to the PISA 2018 framework. Predictors were reduced to 74 variables by excluding (a) non-cognitive/metacognitive and schooling constructs with 100% missing data (since some countries may opt out of non-required questionnaires) and (b) background variables that were used to derive other variables (e.g., parents’ highest education excluded because it was used to derive ESCS). Missing values in the remaining predictors were imputed using an MCMC approach (mice in R) prior to modeling.

main_findings.target_variable: Reading achievement (PISA reading literacy; first plausible value)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression: OOB R² = 0.57; OOB RMSE = 72.26. Hyperparameters: 1,000 trees; 24 predictors per split. Feature selection via 10-fold cross-validation: lowest error rate with top 37 predictors; top-10 importance list reported (MDA-based).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (Singapore; 15-year-olds) the study leveraged metacognition-related variables (assessing credibility and summarizing), perceived reading difficulty, school socioeconomic context (school ESCS mean), and learning time to predict reading achievement, finding that the model explained 57% of the variance (OOB R² = 0.57) with RMSE = 72.26 and that non-cognitive/metacognitive constructs dominated the top predictor rankings. This indicates that strengthening students’ metacognitive reading processes and related motivational/engagement supports may be a high-leverage policy and school-practice target for improving reading literacy, though the results are predictive and not causal and the ML stage used only the first plausible value.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 microdata for Singapore (6,676 students aged 15 nested in 166 schools) and predicts PISA 2018 reading literacy achievement using a Random Forest regression model. The outcome is the PISA reading score represented by plausible values; however, the authors fit the ML model using only the first plausible value rather than aggregating across all 10 PVs. Missing predictor data were imputed using an MCMC approach implemented in R (mice), and predictors were reduced to 74 variables by excluding constructs with 100% missingness and variables redundant with ESCS derivations. The best-tuned Random Forest used 1,000 trees and 24 predictors per split, achieving OOB R² = 0.57 and OOB RMSE = 72.26. Feature importance (MDA) and 10-fold cross-validation indicated the lowest error rate when using the top 37 predictors, with the top predictors heavily concentrated in non-cognitive/metacognitive constructs (e.g., assessing credibility and summarizing) alongside a few schooling and socioeconomic variables. Limitations include the single-PV approach and the lack of explicit reporting on applying PISA sampling/replicate weights in the ML stage.
